    Brova

    A rehearsal partner for Arab actors. It reads every other part in Egyptian Arabic, waits for your line, and gives you a face to look at while you act.

    What Dina told us

    FREQUENCYRehearses every day, alone, by repeating lines.
    PAINNo one to read with, and memorizing takes too long.
    TOP 3Scene Partner, an AI partner with eye contact, script-to-voice conversion.
    FORMATSWord and PDF over WhatsApp. On set: printed pages with last-minute edits.
    AI PARTNERA face she looks at that reacts to her, but reads the lines exactly. No improvising.
    SETUPPhone only, self-tapes on the phone, cloud storage is fine, scripts in Egyptian colloquial.

    She skipped the price question twice. Pricing below is a set of hypotheses to test, not her answer.

    New pages on set → a working scene partner in under a minute.

    Her sharpest pain is new or edited pages arriving on set, with little time before they shoot that scene. A photo of the page becomes a script with characters detected, and the partner starts reading. Nobody in this category is built for that moment in Arabic.

    Who it's for

    • Working actors in Egypt who get scripts late and rehearse alone. Dina is the first design partner.
    • Acting students in Cairo workshops and academies, who drill scenes weekly and rarely have a partner at home.
    • Acting schools as buyers: one purchase covers a whole class, which is how the product reaches students cheaply.
    • Later: actors across the region working in Egyptian, Gulf and Levantine dialects.

    Competition

    AI scene partners already exist in English. Listening for your line and continuing automatically is now standard, so Brova can't win on that feature alone. It wins on Arabic, on paper pages, and on the face.

    AppWhat it doesGap Brova fills
    Rehearsal ProLong-running pro app: highlight lines, record cues, teleprompter, pacing. $19.99.No AI reading; English-first.
    LineLearnerRecord your own cues, import PDF or Word, rehearse in groups. $3.99.You record every other part yourself.
    Linus, CueUp, Script Buddy, Cold ReadAI reads the other characters with distinct voices and waits for your line.English-first. No Egyptian Arabic voices, no handling of Arabic paper pages, no on-screen face.
    BrovaEgyptian Arabic voices, Arabic right-to-left scripts, photos of edited pages, a face placed by the camera.—

    Roadmap

    VersionWhat shipsWhy
    v1Import from Word, PDF, WhatsApp share and photos (text recognition). Automatic character detection. Scene Partner with speed control, pause after each line, scene sections and loop. AI Partner face reading the script exactly. Hiding words as a single setting.Her top 3, plus her two pains.
    v2Flashcards, spaced repetition, a memorization test that checks spoken lines against the script. Recording a real actor's voice as the partner. Self-tape teleprompter and timer.Her original list, after the core is proven.
    v3Dialect and accent training with IPA (Sa'idi, Fallahi, Bedouin dictionaries), two-camera recording, background and lighting fixes.Hardest to build and needs dialect data.

    How it would be built

    • Voice (tested in this prototype): the sample scene is voiced with ElevenLabs Eleven v4 and three Egyptian library voices (Karim, Sawsan, Fatima), with an emotion tag on each line. Library voices need a paid plan through the API (Starter, about $5/month). Azure's Egyptian voices (Salma, Shakir) are the cheaper fallback. Each line is generated once and cached, so repeats cost nothing.
    • Face: a 2D animated character (for example built with Rive) driven by the mouth-shape timing the voice engine returns, plus one emotion per line read from the stage directions (such as بعصبية or بهدوء). No large language model is needed for v1, which matches "reads the lines exactly."
    • Knowing when she's done (built into this prototype): the mic detects that she started speaking, then waits for a silence she can tune (0.6–2.5 s, to allow dramatic pauses) and a minimum speaking time based on the line's length. No speech-to-text needed. Speech-to-text comes later, for the memorization test. The shared prototype page blocks the microphone, so it works in the local or hosted copy and in the real app.
    • Reading the script: each line gets a feeling (from its stage direction, or carried over from the character's last direction) and an intent (question, rhetorical question, exclamation, trailing off). The same analysis writes the voice tags, so for example «أنام؟ وبنتي…» is delivered as an incredulous rhetorical question. In the real app, an AI model would do this reading at import.
    • Talking to a man or a woman: Egyptian scripts write "you" endings the same way, but they're said differently (عملتلك is 3amaltelak to a man and 3amaltelek to a woman; معاك becomes معاكي for a woman). At import, Claude reads the scene once and decides each character's gender, who every line is said to, the feeling and the line type, without asking the actor. The voice then gets the right vowel mark. If Claude isn't available, built-in rules take over («يا ...», «إنتي/إنت», the previous speaker). The sample includes both versions of each affected line.
    • Import: cloud text recognition with Arabic support for photos and PDFs, then a parser for Egyptian script layout: the name on its own line or before a colon, and stage directions in parentheses.
    • App: a single cross-platform codebase (Flutter or React Native), phone-first.

    Pricing hypotheses

    FreeEGP 0One active script, limited voice minutes each week. Long enough to get through a real audition.
    ProEGP 99–149 / monthUnlimited scripts and voices, the AI Partner, photo import. Priced against streaming subscriptions.
    Academyper student / termWorkshops buy seats for a class. Lowers the price per actor and gives a sales channel.

    Risks

    HIGHEgyptian voice quality and cost. The sample scene now uses real Egyptian voices on v4. Dina still has to judge whether they act well enough, and voice cost per active actor has to fit under the subscription price.
    HIGHReading set pages. Photos of printed Arabic with handwritten edits are hard for text recognition. One wrong word breaks memorization.
    MEDScript formats vary. Each production lays out names, directions and parentheticals differently. The editable preview step has to make fixing mistakes quick.
    MEDFace that feels fake. A face that is too realistic can feel creepy. A stylized face is safer and cheaper.
    LOWConfidential scripts. Cloud storage is fine for Dina, but productions under NDA will want an auto-delete option.

    Next two weeks

    1. Voice test: render this scene with Azure Salma/Shakir and two ElevenLabs Egyptian voices. Dina ranks them blind.
    2. Script test: collect 10 real scripts (Word, PDF, photos of edited set pages) and measure text recognition and character detection.
    3. More actors: send the same questionnaire through Dina to 10–15 actors and 1–2 workshops. Ask about price indirectly ("too cheap to trust" / "a stretch") instead of directly.
    4. Hands-on test: let 3 actors use this prototype on their phones and watch where they get stuck.
    Sources: Azure ar-EG Salma · Azure ar-EG Shakir · ElevenLabs Egyptian accent · Backstage: line memorization apps · Rehearsal Pro · Linus · CueUp · Cold Read
